# Analysis: Turtle Trading System 2 (Donchian Breakout) — REJECT

**Why this outcome is consistent with the mechanism.** System 2 is a pure long-term trend-following breakout: it wins big and rarely (win_rate 26.1%, profit_factor 1.32), relying on a handful of extended trends to pay for many small losses. That pattern shows up clearly in the monthly returns — three months (2023-10 at +43.7%, 2024-02 at +35.6%, 2024-06 at +14.4%) drive nearly all the cumulative gain, sitting inside a long stretch of grinding, choppy negative months (Oct-21 through Jun-22, most of 2025). The rolling-annual series confirms this: performance rockets from -42% to +147% by Feb-2024 on the back of that trend cluster, then decays steadily back to negative territory through most of 2025 as breakouts whipsawed. This is exactly the fragility the auditor flagged: in-sample/walk-forward captured the 2023-24 trend window, but the OOS expectancy of -113.67 shows the strategy did not find comparable trends on unseen data — it needs rare, large, sustained moves that didn't recur.

**Dependencies.** Gains concentrated in Capital Goods and Healthcare (+$64.8k, +$30.0k), which alone exceed total P&L; Metals & Mining, IT, Services, Telecom were net drags (-$9.6k to -$13.3k), suggesting sector-specific trend persistence rather than a broad edge. Bearish-regime entries outperformed bullish (+$39.5k vs +$19.2k), unusual for a long-only breakout system and worth scrutiny — possibly reflecting sharp mean-reversion snaps after bearish-day breakdowns rather than genuine trend continuation.

**Follow-ups.** (1) Test regime-conditioning explicitly — did the two winning months coincide with a market-wide breadth expansion that a single-market breakout system can't reliably time again? (2) Given only one asset class here versus the original's 20+ uncorrelated futures markets, a natural next hypothesis is running System 2 across a basket of NSE sectors/indices simultaneously to see if diversification restores the edge that concentration destroyed.

The auditor's rejection is a **sample-size verdict, not a performance verdict** — note the apparent contradiction: the metrics table shows 70 trades with a 2.91 profit factor and 17.46% CAGR, yet the rejection cites "0 total trades" and "0 in holdout." This tells us the 70 trades shown are pooled/aggregate figures that failed to survive the walk-forward window structure — likely because the state-transition qualification proxy for VCP breakout produces so few genuine signals per rolling window that most windows (and the entire holdout) simply never fire. This is consistent with the disclosed caveat that our entry trigger is a raw template-qualification day rather than a true VCP pivot breakout — a rarer, more precisely-timed event — so signal scarcity across the multi-year holdout is expected, not anomalous.

The sector and regime concentration reinforces this fragility: P&L is dominated by Healthcare (+19.3k) and Capital Goods (+10.4k), with Automobile (-3.2k) and Chemicals (-1.8k) dragging negative — a handful of sector bets, not a diversified edge. # Analysis: Cross-Sectional Momentum — REJECT

The in-sample/walk-forward picture looks superficially strong: 224 trades, PF 1.80, Sharpe 0.97, Sortino 2.75, CAGR 23.6%, expectancy +1357.92 per trade. But the auditor's verdict rests on the one number that matters most — **out-of-sample expectancy of -54.02** — meaning the edge the backtest found does not survive on data the model never touched. This is a classic overfitting signature: a momentum ranking system with a 126-day time-stop, no skip period, and single-vintage entries has many degrees of freedom (formation window, ranking universe, sector mix) that can fit in-sample noise without capturing a repeatable cross-sectional effect.

The return concentration corroborates this fragility: monthly returns are dominated by a handful of outsized months (Dec-2023 +70%, Aug-2026 +57%, several +40% months) sitting alongside frequent double-digit negative months (2025 alone gave back -55.6% annually). A strategy with genuine cross-sectional edge shouldn't need a small number of "jackpot" months to carry the whole track record. P&L is also sector-concentrated — Capital Goods (+148k) and Financial Services (+88k) account for the bulk of profit, while Chemicals (-22.6k), Metals & Mining (-16.6k) and Realty (-13.2k) bled steadily — suggesting the model rode a few sector-momentum waves rather than a diversified, structural effect. Regime split (bullish 213k vs bearish 91k) shows it only worked when Nifty was already trending, consistent with momentum being regime-dependent rather than robust.

Follow-up ideas: (1) test the paper's actual overlapping-portfolio (multi-vintage) construction to see if smoothing removes the OOS collapse — single-vintage variance may be masking a real but weaker signal; (2) reintroduce the skip period and re-run OOS specifically on 2025 data, where reversal contamination looks worst.

**Why the verdict is REJECT — and why the sample is uninformative rather than merely "unlucky":**

With only 2 trades in ~2 years (exposure 3.63%, avg hold 27 days), this backtest cannot speak to the low-beta anomaly at all — it's two isolated data points, not a strategy track record. Both trades lost money (Financial Services -953.38, Power -969.18), producing a -961.28 expectancy and -1.92% max drawdown on capital. Notably, one loss occurred in a "bullish" Nifty regime and one in "bearish" — with n=2 this tells us nothing about regime dependency, it's simply too small to distinguish signal from noise. The rolling-annual view shows 11 months of flat 0.0% (no trade active) before both losses land in the same overlapping window, consistent with a single-vintage, low-turnover selection process rather than any repeated edge being tested.

Mechanically, trade scarcity is expected: this backtest only captures the long, unlevered, low-beta stock-selection leg (disclosed scope reduction) — the paper's actual claim requires a levered, beta-neutral long/short pairing with the high-beta short leg, which isn't implementable here (no NSE SLB, no margin). Combined with the 1-year (vs. paper's 5-year) volatility/correlation lookback — a disclosed deviation forced by the platform's frozen 3-year recency gate — beta estimates are noisier and the eligible-stock universe passing low-beta screens in any given window is apparently very thin, hence just 2 trades.

**Follow-ups regardless of verdict:** (1) Relax the single-vintage constraint to overlapping monthly rebalancing to generate more independent trade observations from the same underlying signal. (2) Test whether the low-beta screen threshold is too strict for NSE's cap-weighted universe under a 1-year window, producing near-empty eligible sets — widening the beta percentile bands may be needed to get a testable sample size before any verdict beyond REJECT is possible.

# Analysis: Betting Against Beta — Why REJECT

**Mechanism mismatch drove the outcome.** This backtest measures only the long, unlevered, low-beta stock-selection leg — not the paper's actual claim (a leverage-scaled, beta-neutral long-low-beta/short-high-beta spread). With just 209 trades collapsed into a single walk-forward window, the auditor correctly flagged 0/1 positive-expectancy windows as statistically meaningless — one sample cannot distinguish skill from noise, exactly the SEED-ORB-2 trap. A profit factor of 1.095 and Sharpe of 0.308 sit in marginal, unconvincing territory even before the single-window problem.

**Regime dependence:** the strategy actually did *better* in bearish regimes (P&L 4,332 vs. 3,266 bullish) — intuitively consistent with low-beta stocks cushioning drawdowns — but this defensive character is precisely what a long-only construction can't monetize the way the paper intends (which profits from shorting high-beta simultaneously). The monthly return series shows no stable pattern (7 losing months of 23, including a -8.98% March 2026), consistent with a weak, regime-dependent signal rather than a robust anomaly.

**Sector concentration:** gains clustered in Healthcare, Textiles, and Auto (4,566 / 3,638 / 3,312) while Capital Goods, Chemicals, Services, and Construction Materials bled over -1,100 to -2,571 each — suggesting the "low-beta" signal is really proxying for defensive-sector membership rather than a cross-sectional beta effect, which would explain fragility across a single window.

**Follow-up ideas:** (1) Test sector-neutralized beta ranking to isolate whether the edge is genuinely beta-driven or sector-driven; (2) if infrastructure ever supports SLB/leverage, re-test the true beta-neutral spread — the long-only leg alone was never expected to carry the paper's full documented return.

# Analysis: Betting Against Beta — REJECT

The verdict rests on one dominant fact: out-of-sample expectancy is -4.88/trade despite a rosy full-sample expectancy of +175.4 and rolling annual returns that peaked near +49% in mid-2024. This is a textbook in-sample/regime-decay pattern, not noise — the strategy's fortunes track the 2023-2024 bull run almost exactly (rolling annual return climbs from ~6% in Jan-2023 to ~49% by Jul-2024) and then deteriorates sharply from late-2024 onward (rolling annual return falls to -11.8% by Oct-2025), coinciding with sharp monthly drawdowns (Oct-24: -9.3%, Feb-25: -9.2%, Mar-26: -16.1%). The P&L-by-regime split (bullish 64,714 vs bearish 5,270) confirms the edge was never really "low-beta outperformance" in a risk-managed sense — it was a long-only, unlevered equity book that made money because Indian equities rallied, and low-beta names simply rode that rally with less drag. Once the tailwind faded, the walk-forward/OOS window exposed the strategy as having no genuine standalone edge. This is consistent with the disclosed scope gap: without the paper's leverage-scaled, beta-neutral construction, you're only capturing the long low-beta leg, which the paper itself predicts is the smaller, directionally-exposed half of the true factor — exactly the kind of construction that looks fine in a bull sample and fails once beta stops being a good proxy for "safety" in a genuinely new period. Sector data reinforces market-beta dependence rather than idiosyncratic stock-picking skill: gains concentrated in cyclical/consumer-discretionary sectors (Auto 21k, Consumer Services 11.9k, Financial Services 10.6k) that thrive in risk-on tapes, while defensive/rate-sensitive FMCG (-6.4k) and Chemicals (-3.2k) — sectors that should theoretically benefit from a true low-beta premium in a chop/down market — actually lost money. That is the opposite of what a working low-beta anomaly should show in a weak-regime OOS slice.

Follow-ups for a future hypothesis: (1) Test a genuine long-short or at least a long/cash market-neutral overlay (e.g., inverse-index futures proxy) once short/leverage infrastructure exists, to isolate the factor from beta-1 market direction — this result cannot distinguish "low beta works" from "long equities worked in 2023-24." (2) Re-run the 1-year lookback sensitivity explicitly against a 3-year window on a longer available history outside the frozen recency gate, to check whether the shortened vol/correlation window is amplifying the late-sample beta misclassification (i.e., stocks whose realized beta jumped after the 2024 rally may have been mis-sorted as "low beta" heading into the 2025 drawdown).
